tier_reason: First-party 'Example Output' blocks in the author's SpeedTestCV repo (boofcv/readme.md JMH table, opencv/readme.md script output); benchmark code is public (boofcv/src/jmh/java/speed/BenchmarkImageProcessing.java, opencv/benchmark.py) but no CPU model or hardware is stated and the outputs predate the pinned versions, so C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: The two example outputs were written in commit 0bd58bd (2019-03-21) and never re-run: BoofCV 0.33.1 (build.gradle at that commit) under JMH 1.19, 3 warm-up and 5 measurement iterations, 1 fork, BoofConcurrency.USE_CONCURRENT=true; OpenCV side opencv-python and opencv-contrib-python 4.0.0.21 with numpy 1.16.2 (requirements.txt at that commit), timed by opencv/benchmark.py as the mean of 10 time.time() trials (1 for histogram). The current build.gradle (0.38-SNAPSHOT, JDK 14 source level) and requirements.txt (4.5.1.48) were bumped in March 2020/2021 commits that changed only the run commands and the SIFT prose, not the numbers. JDK version not stated beyond 'JDK 1.8 and JDK 11 produce similar output'.
corrections.workload: SpeedTestCV example output on one large chessboard JPEG (gray) and one binary PNG: BoofCV 0.33.1 under JMH (avgt, 5 iterations, ms/op, concurrency on) against OpenCV 4.0.0.21 Python calls timed by a script (ms per call, multi-threaded as shipped). Operations: Gaussian blur radius 5, Sobel, local mean threshold radius 5, histogram, Canny edge chains, external contours, Shi-Tomasi corners, polar Hough lines.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed result, ratios derived from page data (OpenCV ms divided by BoofCV ms, from the two readme example outputs, both dated 2019-03-21). BoofCV faster: good features 38.313 ms vs 277.2 ms (7.2x), Hough polar 743.051 ms vs 3086.3 ms (4.2x, not like-for-like, see caveats), histogram 2.268 ms vs 7.0 ms (3.1x), external contour 47.055 ms vs 83.3 ms (1.8x), Sobel 8.010 ms vs 14.0 ms (1.7x). BoofCV slower: Gaussian blur 36.139 ms vs 12.1 ms (OpenCV 3.0x faster), Canny 142.658 ms vs 61.7 ms (OpenCV 2.3x faster), local mean threshold 20.495 ms vs 15.4 ms (OpenCV 1.3x faster). No OpenCV row for SIFT or SURF (the 2019 run printed 'Skipping SIFT and SURF. Not installed').
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence for a catalogue entry in this category: the numbers are 'Example Output' blocks in two sub-readmes of the author's SpeedTestCV repo (4 stars, no license file, last commit 2022-07-28), not a published results table; hardware and CPU model are not stated (the BoofCV block says 'On my system'). Both blocks date from commit 0bd58bd (2019-03-21) and measure BoofCV 0.33.1 against opencv-python 4.0.0.21; the later version bumps to BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT and opencv-python 4.5.1.48 did not refresh them (the current benchmark.py would print a SIFT row and a different row order and 2-decimal format). BoofCV is timed with JMH (with warm-up, concurrency enabled), OpenCV with a hand-written Python loop (mean of 10 time.time() trials after gc.collect, one trial for the histogram, no warm-up, Python call overhead included); cv2.setNumThreads(0) is commented out, so OpenCV runs multi-threaded as shipped. Rows are not all like-for-like: OpenCV HoughLines is fed the raw grayscale chessboard image (every non-zero pixel votes), whereas BoofCV's houghPolar computes a gradient and keeps only edges above threshold 50 first, so the 4.2x Hough row compares different work; Shi-Tomasi parameters were tuned separately per library; the OpenCV Canny row includes a findContours call while BoofCV's Canny includes a mandatory blur; the libraries also convert RGB to gray differently (weighted vs plain average). The benchmark file itself lists TODOs. The comparison is not a win overall: OpenCV is 2-3x faster on Gaussian blur and Canny. None of the rows is a colour conversion or resampler, so the assigned category fits only loosely (Gaussian blur and Sobel are the nearest; general image processing would fit better). The author's fuller page, boofcv.org Performance:OpenCV:BoofCV, is blocked in this environment (EGRESS_BLOCKED, confirmed 2026-10-07) and was not read. A 2012 SURF paper by the BoofCV author (title only, not opened; arXiv blocked) reportedly compares SURF runtimes of several implementations; nothing from it is used here. Retier idea for a session with arXiv or boofcv.org access.

notes: Numbers match the two readmes exactly, but git history shows both example outputs were written on 2019-03-21 (BoofCV 0.33.1 vs opencv-python 4.0.0.21) and never re-run, so the record's 0.38-SNAPSHOT / 4.5.1.48 pairing was wrong and is corrected. Shortcomings to record: no hardware stated, JMH vs Python time.time() harness, Hough row not like-for-like (OpenCV votes on the raw gray image), OpenCV faster on blur, Canny and mean threshold, category fit loose. License Apache-2.0, 1.2k stars, last commit 2026-10-06 confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party README Performance table backed by public benchmark code (packages/canvas-txt/bench/compare.mjs), but the CPU model ('Apple Silicon' only) and Node version are not stated, so C, not A.

corrections.caveats: Benchmark code is public (packages/canvas-txt/bench/compare.mjs, read in full) but the CPU model, Node version and run-to-run variance are not stated, so tier C rather than A; one performance.now() total per contender, no repeated runs. It times line-wrapping and measurement only (splitText; the script's layoutText row is not in the README table), not drawing, and not node-canvas fillText, so the lead's second baseline is not measured. The README's feature table says 'faster than canvas-hypertxt on every workload', but its own Performance table shows canvas-hypertxt faster on repeated identical text (0.9 vs 1.1 µs/op), and the README admits hypertxt's estimation mode is faster on long never-seen strings. Cache handling favours canvas-txt: the script clears only canvas-hypertxt's cache before each contender (hyperClearCache), while canvas-txt's module-level per-font width cache and layout memo are never cleared, so in the never-repeating scenario canvas-txt starts with the numeric prefixes and vocabulary already measured by the earlier 100-character pass and Scenario B, whereas hypertxt gets only its 100 warm-up iterations. The never-repeating scenario also keeps the vocabulary warm (about 70 distinct lorem-ipsum words). README numbers are for 600 characters; the script also runs 100 and 1000. The script prints a line-count sanity check (v5 vs hypertxt) whose output is not reported. Lead said issue #13 holds these numbers: it does not, issue #13 is an unrelated request to return the computed text height. The v5 rewrite and recent commits (all 2026-08-10) are co-authored with an AI assistant. Not C++ (TypeScript); baseline is another JavaScript library, so no std comparison applies.

notes: README table numbers match the record exactly (1.1/0.9, 5.6/48.3, 51.3/566.2 µs/op; v4 1,566/1,423/1,382). Shortcomings to record: no CPU model or Node version, README 'faster on every workload' contradicted by its own same-text row, benchmark clears only the baseline's cache (canvas-txt's width cache stays warm across scenarios), wrapping only, single run. MIT, 540 stars, last commit 2026-08-10 confirmed; canvas-hypertxt is already a listed entry.

tier_reason: README makes only prose claims relative to ScanFT (single-thread parity within 1-2 percent, ScanT faster with more threads); no measured numbers are published anywhere in the repo, so D.

corrections.caveats: No measured results anywhere in the repo or README, so the speedup is a prose claim (tier D). The benchmarks in scant_test.go and scans_test.go only vary ScanT's thread count and ScanS; ScanFT appears only in commented-out test code and x/image/vector is absent, so none of the named baselines is timed. The gradient benchmarks (RunGradsT, RunGradsS) draw a fixed 50 times and ignore b.N, so the ns/op that go test would print for them is not a valid per-iteration time. The README's own claim for single-threaded ScanS is parity (within 1-2 percent of ScanFT), not a win; ScanT with one thread is said to be about 10 percent slower, and only ScanT at several threads is said to be faster, with no hardware, Go version or crossover thread count. The lead's other baselines (golang.org/x/image/vector, scanx, FreeType ftgrays itself) are not compared; ScanFT is the nearest relative of ftgrays. Repository has 1 star, 0 forks, 11 commits, last commit 2022-01-17, 'go 1.17' module, so it is old and unmaintained. Not notable on its own; kept at tier D under the keep-and-document rule.

notes: Record is accurate: prose-only parity/multi-thread claim vs ScanFT, no numbers, MIT, 1 star, last commit 2022-01-17 (abandoned). Shortcomings to record: no measurements, baselines never timed in the benchmark files, gradient benchmarks ignore b.N, single-thread result is parity not a win, not notable. Distinct from the listed srwiley/scanx (different repo), not a duplicate.
